overview: This file combines a U.S. Embassy London despatch and three British economic-warfare enclosures concerning Japan’s wartime shortage of industrial diamonds with a separate State Department memorandum on Japanese ferrous metallurgy. The diamond correspondence assesses the limited output available from occupied Borneo and Java, the pre-occupation flooding of the Martapura fields and evacuation of diamond stocks, shortages of skilled cutters, and Japan’s inability to obtain anything close to the estimated 250,000–400,000 carats required annually by its war industries. The final document summarizes a Russian-language analysis concluding that shortages of ore, coal, scrap, and production facilities would prevent Japan, Korea, and Manchuria from substantially increasing their 1941 iron and steel output. Despite the file title’s reference to radium, none of the surviving documents concerns radium directly.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 8900 on industrial diamonds for Japan
subfiles.from: Don C. Bliss, Acting Commercial Attaché, U.S. Embassy London
subfiles.about: Transmits British economic-warfare correspondence about industrial diamonds available to Japan from occupied Borneo and related supply questions.
subfiles.summary: Bliss forwards three enclosures received from the chairman of the British Ministry of Economic Warfare’s Diamond Committee. He states that they contain information potentially useful to the Board of Economic Warfare concerning Borneo’s diamond production, Japan’s industrial requirements, and associated wartime supply issues.

subfiles.title: Reading letter on Borneo diamond production and Japanese requirements
subfiles.from: J. L. Reading, Ministry of Economic Warfare
subfiles.about: Evaluates whether the occupied Martapura fields could supply a significant share of Japan’s industrial-diamond requirements.
subfiles.summary: Reading encloses reports from Cairo concerning the flooding of the Martapura diamond fields and the Japanese occupation of Sumatra and Borneo. He reports Borneo production of 2,287 carats in 1939 and 4,219 in 1935, against an estimated Japanese annual requirement of at least 250,000 and possibly 400,000 carats. Although a Board of Economic Warfare estimate suggested that extreme measures might produce 30,000 carats annually, Reading considers even that figure implausibly high.

subfiles.title: Owen letter conveying Larkins’s comments on diamond denial
subfiles.from: Rowland Owen, Office of the Minister of State, Cairo
subfiles.to: E. J. Holford-Strevens, Ministry of Economic Warfare
subfiles.about: Reports Larkins’s assessment of why Japan could not readily obtain or prepare industrial diamonds from occupied Southeast Asia.
subfiles.summary: Larkins interprets Japan’s apparent industrial-diamond shortage as evidence that flooding the Martapura fields and evacuating known stocks from Java to Ceylon and Australia had been effective. He suggests that Japan may also lack the expertise required to prepare industrial diamonds, since European cutters in Java and Martapura were interned and local cutters might be unable or unwilling to work without European supervision. He adds that efforts prevented the Japanese consul at Surabaya from acquiring diamonds.

subfiles.title: Larkins minute on Sumatra, Borneo, and Netherlands East Indies diamonds
subfiles.from: L. B. S. Larkins, Commercial Secretary, Cairo
subfiles.about: Comments on Japanese control of Sumatra and the availability, grading, and possible export of diamonds from occupied Java and Borneo.
subfiles.summary: Larkins doubts that Japan can easily control or settle eastern Sumatra, citing reported revolt in Aceh, although he expects strong occupation of Medan and fortification of Palembang. He asks which diamonds might be involved in a proposed transaction with Switzerland and notes that the Martapura and Java fields were flooded before occupation. He questions whether Japan possesses the experts needed to grade Netherlands East Indies diamonds and identifies Aaron Gutwirth, Konsommer, and several others as possible cutters remaining in Java. Larkins believes Gutwirth has personal and family reasons not to assist Japan, since relatives were in Allied-influenced Maputo and Australia.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on Japanese ferrous metallurgy
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Russian-language article assessing wartime iron and steel production and resource constraints in Japan, Korea, and Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum refers to Kuibyshev Despatch No. 270 and its translation of an article titled “Ferrous Metallurgy in Japan Under War Conditions.” The article estimates combined 1941 production in Japan, Korea, and Manchuria at 4.5 million tons of pig iron and 7 million tons of steel, with pig-iron capacity of 8 million tons. After reviewing iron ore, coal, scrap, and production capabilities, its author concludes that Japan lacks the materials and facilities needed to increase iron and steel output appreciably above 1941 levels.

interest: The file offers unusually concrete comparisons between Japan’s vast estimated industrial-diamond demand and the very small output available from occupied Borneo, making it useful for measuring the effectiveness of Allied strategic-materials denial. Particularly revealing are the accounts of flooding mines, evacuating stocks, obstructing the Japanese consul at Surabaya, and assessing whether interned European cutters—or named individuals whose families were within Allied reach—would cooperate with Japan. The juxtaposition of these diamond reports with a memorandum on iron and steel constraints, all under a file title referring to radium, also illustrates the heterogeneous and sometimes imperfect character of the State Department’s decimal filing system.
